summary: Weekly POC sync to review quantization experiment results (INT8 vs FP8). Redwood presented updated quality metrics and perf deltas; FP8 shows ~1-1.5% QA delta vs baseline with 30-40% throughput improvement in some configs. INT8 lowers mem/cost more but has edge-case quality regressions on long-context prompts. Discussed next steps: deeper evaluation on Argus traces, private benchmark, and pricing for Dedicated with FP8 profile.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lydia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (Argus ML Eng), Tom Reynolds (Argus Platform), Priya Shah (Argus Security)

[00:00] Lydia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to 45. Quick agenda: results recap from our INT8 / FP8 runs, perf deltas, quality review on your sample prompts, and next steps for the private benchmark. Marcus, do you want to kick off with the numbers?

[00:20] Marcus Patel: Yeah, sure. So hi, Sara, Tom, Priya. We ran the latest set against the 1,200-sample eval you gave us — the bank customer support and transaction audit prompts — and compared baseline FP16 against INT8 and FP8 quantized variants. High-level: FP8 looks promising, roughly 30 to 40 percent throughput increase in our Dedicated configs, latency down about 20 to 35% depending on batch. INT8 gives more memory savings but we saw a few quality regressions on longer context prompts.

[01:00] Sara Gomez: When you say "quality regressions", can you give an example? Like is it hallucination or just slightly worse NLG?

[01:10] Marcus Patel: Mostly semantic drift on long-form follow-ups — e.g., when the prompt references earlier transaction IDs across a long conversation we saw the model occasionally drop prior context or substitute numbers. It's not catastrophic but it shows up in the QA metrics. For short prompts (<= 128 tokens) INT8 is basically identical.

[01:40] Tom Reynolds: Is that the "K V cash" issue or KV cache — sorry, transcription — I mean, does this relate to kv cache alignment on quantized kernels?

[01:50] Marcus Patel: Good call. It's related to kv-cache numeric precision differences and also tokenization edge cases in a few of the samples. FP8 keeps more dynamic range so it's more stable for those long-chain context references. We did also see occasional noise when we forced high batching — batch 16 on 32k model bits was worse.

[02:20] Lydia Chen: To add to that, the FP8 profile we shipped uses a mixed-kernel path in our runtime — it's a bit newer, tuned for long context, while INT8 currently uses a more aggressive quant matrix so you get more compression but a bit more variance.

[02:40] Priya Shah: From a security/compliance perspective, does FP8 require any different key management or logging? Our compliance team will want to know if we need new attestations.

[02:50] Marcus Patel: No changes to KMS or audit logs; it's purely a runtime/compute format. All data-in-transit and at-rest still uses the same encryption controls. We'll include a note in the security packet clarifying that FP8 is a compute-only change.

[03:10] Priya Shah: Okay that's good. Please include the kernel list and the CPU/GPU driver versions you tested on. We saw last time some variance depending on ML driver version.

[03:20] Marcus Patel: Will do. We tested on A100s with CUDA 12.2 and on a small RTX class in the internal lab for comparatives; I'll enumerate exact kernels.

[03:30] Sara Gomez: What about perplexity or QA-style metrics? You said FP8 is 1 to 1.5% delta — what's the metric?

[03:40] Marcus Patel: Right, so for your QA task we used exact match and F1 and also human-rated pass/fail on a 200-sample subset. INT8 had a ~2.5% absolute drop in exact-match on the long-context set, FP8 was around 0.8 to 1.5% absolute drop depending on prompt template. On short-context categories both are <0.5% delta.

[04:10] Lydia Chen: To be clear those are absolute percentage points; relative percent depends on baseline. We'll share the raw CSVs so you can slice by template.

[04:20] Tom Reynolds: On perf, you said 30-40% throughput improvement for FP8 — is that versus FP16 or INT8? And under what batching?

[04:30] Marcus Patel: Versus FP16 baseline in Dedicated configs with a moderate batching profile (batch 4 typical, 8 for non-latency). With batch 1 (latency sensitive) we saw ~15-20% improvement; with batch 8 it went up to mid 30s. INT8 can hit slightly higher throughput but at the tradeoff of the regressions we discussed.

[05:00] Sara Gomez: For our use case latency at batch 1 matters — the payment confirmation flow is very sensitive. So if FP8 gives 15-20% at batch 1 with only ~1% quality impact that's attractive.

[05:12] Marcus Patel: Exactly — FP8 is kind of the sweet spot for latency-critical workloads. Also it's more stable across long contexts.

[05:20] Lydia Chen: Quick note on cost: because FP8 allows higher packing / less memory per token, the per-token GPU cost goes down; we'll include an illustrative cost delta in the pricing doc for Dedicated.

[05:35] Tom Reynolds: Great. On the private deployment question, will the same FP8 kernels be available in our VPC/on-prem package? We may need HSM integrations too.

[05:45] Marcus Patel: Yes, same kernels. For Private we ship the identical runtime; if you're on-prem the only differences are packaging and management plane connectivity. HSM/KMS integrations remain the same, and audit logs are preserved. We'll surface the kernel manifest and driver compatibility notes.

[06:10] Priya Shah: On the kernel manifest please include versions and checksums, that helps our security team validate supply chain.

[06:18] Marcus Patel: Noted — will add checksums.

[06:25] Sara Gomez: Did you run any adversarial or edge-case prompts to surface hallucinations? We have regulatory scripts that are a bit adversarial.

[06:35] Marcus Patel: We ran the internal adversarial set and saw a slight uplift in hallucination rate for INT8 on a 200-sample set; FP8 was effectively at parity. We'll include the exact items where INT8 failed so you can review.

[06:55] Lydia Chen: Okay, let's talk about the concrete bench we recommended: a 10k-run using your production traces, batch 1 and batch 4 splits, and both FP8/INT8 runs plus FP16 baseline. Tom, can you do the trace export?

[07:12] Tom Reynolds: Yes, we can extract a 10k request sample that mirrors the payment flow and some customer support flows. I can have that by Friday, 2026-09-25.

[07:22] Lydia Chen: Awesome—then Marcus will run the private benchmark the week of 09-29 and we'll share logs and the eval spreadsheet by 09-24.

[07:30] Marcus Patel: For the private benchmark we'll spin up Dedicated-like infra in our staging and replicate the kernel stack your environment will have. We'll capture latency p95/p99, throughput, token-level cost, and the model outputs for QA.

[07:45] Sara Gomez: For evaluation, can you add a human-review column and also give us the raw logits for the samples that failed? That helps our team debug.

[07:55] Marcus Patel: Yeah we can include logits for failed cases, can't include everything due to size but we'll provide the subset you flag.

[08:05] Priya Shah: About telemetry — what level of logs do you need? We prefer not to send PII; we'll scrub customer identifiers.

[08:14] Lydia Chen: Please scrub PII, replace with synthetic IDs. Token-level traces and timings are sufficient; remove account numbers. We'll accept anonymized traces.

[08:25] Tom Reynolds: On pricing: if we go Dedicated with FP8 tuned profile what's the delta vs standard FP16 Dedicated?

[08:34] Lydia Chen: We'll provide a sample pricing sheet. Ballpark: because FP8 increases throughput it can reduce per-request GPU time 20-35%, so the effective cost per call falls similarly. But we'll send an itemized estimate for your call volume.

[08:50] Sara Gomez: One more technical question — how does Redwood handle fallback? If we see quality regression in production can we automatically route to FP16?

[08:59] Marcus Patel: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based fallbacks. You can route by route or by confidence score; we can set an automatic fallback to FP16 if a metric threshold is breached.

[09:12] Lydia Chen: We'll include a proposed fallback policy in the rollout doc so it's clear how we handle gradual ramps.

[09:20] Priya Shah: On the compliance docs — we need SOC2 type II evidence and a note on your kernel signing. Also a list of who had access to the private runtime.

[09:30] Lydia Chen: We'll include SOC2 artifacts and kernel signing details. Marcus will append the kernel manifest and access list.

[09:40] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood's side to run the 10k private benchmark?

[09:46] Marcus Patel: No blockers. Need the trace export and confirm compute profile (A100 v4 vs A100 v2) — that affects perf numbers.

[09:55] Tom Reynolds: We'll indicate the infra, but we'll probably mirror A100 v4.

[10:00] Lydia Chen: Alright let's recap next steps quickly...

[10:05] Lydia Chen: Action recap: 1) Lydia to share eval spreadsheet and FP8/INT8 raw outputs by 09-24. 2) Tom to provide anonymized 10k trace by 09-25. 3) Marcus to run the private benchmark week of 09-29 and return perf logs and outputs by 10-01. 4) Priya to confirm compliance doc list by 09-28. 5) Redwood to send Dedicated FP8 pricing by 09-25.

[10:35] Sara Gomez: That timeline works for us. Happy to sync mid-week if anything changes.

[10:42] Priya Shah: Thanks, helps to have the kernel checksums too.

[10:48] Marcus Patel: Noted on checksums and driver versions.

[10:52] Lydia Chen: Cool — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts and invite for the private benchmark kickoff.

[10:58] Tom Reynolds: Thanks, bye.

[11:00] (call ends)
